7.1.b:
Every total knee copies a joint that is neither a pure hinge nor symmetrical, so anatomy comes first.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what knee anatomy matters for a total knee?"
- "The knee is a **modified hinge**: it rolls back in flexion and screws home in extension."
- "It is asymmetric: the tibia sits in **3° varus**, and the medial plateau and condyle are larger."
- "The collaterals and corners guide balancing; the **PCL** decides CR or PS."

### Joint Type and Kinematics
The knee moves in three planes, and that is why a fixed hinge fails.

#### Degrees of Freedom
- The knee is a **synovial** modified hinge (a condyloid joint)
- An oval condyle sits in an ellipsoid cavity, so motion is multiplanar
- It has two tibiofemoral compartments and one patellofemoral compartment
- It moves with **3 degrees of freedom** (Prof Abd Elkarim)
[[FIG: Fig 7.1 · 7.1
- Flexion–extension is the main one; rotation and abduction–adduction are smaller
- So a **fixed hinge**, which blocks rotation, overloads fixation: it is salvage only

#### Motion in Gait
- The knee flexes ≈**70°** in swing and ≈20° in stance (Campbell)
- Abduction–adduction reaches ≈10°, and rotation 10–15°

#### Rollback and Screw-Home
- In flexion the **medial** condyle stays while the lateral condyle rolls back
- Posterior translation is **2 mm** medially but 21 mm laterally (Campbell)
- This **medial pivot** is the basis of medial-pivot designs
- In terminal extension the tibia rotates externally and locks: **screw-home**
- The **popliteus** unlocks it

MEMORY HOOK — the dancer's heel
- In flexion the medial condyle is a dancer's planted heel (**2 mm**); the lateral condyle swings round it (**21 mm**).

### Tibial Surface
The two plateaus are unequal, and that shapes the cuts, the tray cover and the film.

#### Plateaus and Alignment
- The **medial plateau** is oval, larger and concave
- The **lateral plateau** is round, smaller, and flat to convex
- The proximal tibia normally sits in **3° varus** to the mechanical axis (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- Arthritis hits the **medial** compartment most, so most candidates are **varus**

#### Tray Coverage
- The medial condyle is larger and sits more posteriorly
- So a symmetrical tray leaves the **posteromedial** tibia uncovered
[[FIG: Fig 7.2 · 7.1

#### Eminence and Menisci
- On a true lateral film, the concave medial and convex lateral outlines show the **posterior slope**
- Front to back, the eminence carries: medial anterior root, **ACL**, lateral roots, medial posterior root, **PCL**
- The medial meniscus is fixed to the deep MCL and capsule; the lateral one is mobile
- So medial meniscal tears are commoner

### Femoral Surface
The femur mirrors the tibia: the medial condyle is bigger, and the back of both condyles decides flexion.

#### Condyles
- The **medial condyle** is wider, more distal and more posterior
- It projects posteriorly in flexion and distally in extension (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- So it compensates the 3° tibial varus
- It carries **75%** of body weight (Handbook)
- The weight-bearing axis passes a few millimetres medial to the knee centre
- The lateral compartment works more in rotation, so it needs less width
- A tibia cut at 90° then leaves a trapezoidal flexion gap → 08 Technique (3° rotation)

#### Posterior Condylar Offset
- From the side, each condyle bulges a little in front and a lot behind
- This posterior bulge is the **posterior condylar offset**, and it allows deep flexion
- If it is not restored, the tibia impinges early
[[FIG: Fig 7.3 · 7.1
- Then flexion is lost and the polyethylene wears faster
- On the lateral film, offset is the distance from the posterior cortex line to the condyle's back
- The rule is removed = replaced: compare the pre- and postoperative films

#### Trochlea, Notch and Deformity
- The anterior **trochlear groove** is seen on the skyline (Merchant) view
- The posterior **intercondylar notch** is seen on the tunnel view
- A valgus or rheumatoid knee has a **hypoplastic lateral condyle**, distally and posteriorly (Prof Abd Elkarim)
[[FIG: Fig 7.4 · 7.1
- So the posterior condylar axis is unreliable there; use the transepicondylar axis
- A varus knee erodes the posterior **medial** condyle more
- Femoral rotation in the valgus knee → 08 Technique

### Patellar Surface
The patella has its own asymmetry, and it decides where the button goes.

#### Facets
- Ridges divide the patella into **6 facets**
- The lateral facet is larger and the medial smaller; each has superior, middle and inferior parts
- The large lateral facet meets the higher lateral trochlear wall, so it resists lateral shift
- The **odd facet** is the bare medial edge; it touches the medial condyle only beyond 120° (Handbook)

#### Button Position
- The ridge lies **medial**, so the button is placed slightly medial (Prof Sherif Khaled)
[[FIG: Fig 7.5 · 7.1
- Patellar resurfacing → 08 Technique

#### Examination Points
- Patellar cartilage is **thickest** in the body
- **Wiberg** classifies patellar shape by medial versus lateral facet size, on the axial view

### Extra-articular Ligaments
Four groups hold the knee from outside: the coronary ligaments, the collaterals, the two corners and the patellar tendon.

#### Main Structures
| Structure | Course | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Superficial MCL** (medial collateral ligament) | medial epicondyle → 7–10 cm below the joint line | main valgus restraint |
| **Deep MCL** | meniscofemoral + meniscotibial (= coronary) parts | midmedial capsule |
| **POL** (posterior oblique ligament) | adductor tubercle → tibia + posterior capsule | key posteromedial corner |
| **FCL** (fibular collateral = LCL) | lateral epicondyle → fibular head, ≈70 mm | varus restraint at 0–30° |
| **Popliteofibular** | popliteus tendon → fibula | ties the fibula to the femur |
| **Arcuate** | condensation of popliteus-origin fibres | not a separate ligament |

- The **coronary** ligament ties the meniscus to the proximal tibia, like a crown
- It also anchors the meniscus to the capsule

#### Role in Arthroplasty
- The posterior **capsule** at both corners is the main hyperextension restraint; the cruciates are minor
- The superficial MCL inserts deep to the **pes anserinus**
- So a subperiosteal release lengthens it step by step
- In varus the medial side is contracted; in valgus the lateral side is
- A **saw injury to the MCL** needs primary repair or a more constrained implant

### Intra-articular Ligaments
Inside the joint, the PCL and its two companions explain the CR design and two classic traps.
[[FIG: Fig 7.6 · 7.1

#### PCL and Meniscofemoral Ligaments
- The **PCL** is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation
- The **meniscofemoral** ligaments run from the lateral meniscal posterior horn to the medial femoral condyle
- They are variably present: **Humphry** in front of the PCL, **Wrisberg** behind it (Campbell)
- Together they equal ≈**22%** of the PCL's area
- With the popliteus, they tie the lateral meniscus, so it follows the condyle and tears less

#### Diagnostic Traps
- In an isolated PCL tear, an intact Humphry mimics an intact PCL
- So the drawer is small in internal rotation
- On sagittal MRI, the dot in front of or behind the PCL mimics a loose body or meniscal tear
- In a PS knee these ligaments are gone, so only the **cam and post** stop posterior sliding

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Modified hinge · tibia 3° varus · big medial condyle · ridge medial · Humphry front, Wrisberg back**

7.2.b:
With the anatomy in mind, the next question is how a prosthesis copies it: its history, its parts and its constraint.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how did knee designs evolve, and what is constraint?"
- "Resection, interposition, hinges, then the **total condylar knee (Insall, 1973)**: the benchmark."
- "Four parts: femur, tibial tray, **polyethylene insert** (the weak link) and patellar button."
- "More **constraint** means more stability, less motion and more stress on fixation."

### Historical Development
Each era solved one problem and exposed the next.

#### Milestones
| Date | Person | Step |
|---|---|---|
| 1861 | **Ferguson** | resection arthroplasty (osteophytes trimmed only) |
| 1863 | **Verneuil** | interposition (capsule flap) |
| 19th century | **Gluck** | first prosthesis, in ivory |
| 1900–1950 | — | interposition of fat, fascia, skin, cellophane, nylon |
| 1947 | **Judet** | acrylic prostheses |
| 1950s | — | metal components |
| 1960s | **MacIntosh, McKeever** | partial tibial and patellar prostheses |
| ≈1970 | **Freeman–Swanson** (ICLH) | condylar metal-on-polyethylene resurfacing |
| 1973 | **Insall** | **total condylar** knee: the first geometric knee |

#### Lessons from History
- Resection gave motion without stability; hinges gave stability without durability
- The condylar knee gave both
- Johnston, then Freeman–Swanson, put a metal femur on a polyethylene tibia
- This avoided metal-on-metal friction
- Early fixed hinges (**Walldius**, **Shiers**) put all stress on the interface
- So they loosened and became infected

#### The Total Condylar Legacy
- The total condylar knee survived **95%** at 15 years (Campbell)
- It still survived **91%** at 21–23 years
- Its descendants are the **Insall-Burstein** PS knee (1978) and most current designs
- Its tibia was all-polyethylene, and unbacked polyethylene deformed and wore fast
- So metal-backed trays came next, and they reduced deformation and wear
- Patellofemoral reoperations in the late 1980s–1990s brought longer trochleas and asymmetric anterior flanges

### Standard Components
A modern knee has four parts, and one of them wears.

#### The Four Parts
| Component | Design |
|---|---|
| **Femoral** | two convex runners joined by an anterior patellar flange |
| **Tibial tray** | one-piece metal with two dished surfaces |
| **Polyethylene insert** | locks into the tray |
| **Patellar button** | polyethylene dome |

#### The Polyethylene Insert
- The insert is the wear part, so its thickness, conformity and locking decide longevity
- Polyethylene is **radiolucent**, so the metal-to-metal gap on the film is the insert
- Asymmetric narrowing of that gap means wear → 10 TKA radiographs
- Polyethylene and other bearing materials → 01 Bearings

#### Insert Slope and Sizing
- A **built-in slope** makes the insert thicker in front
- A flat insert needs the slope cut in bone
- Size steps fell from 6–8 mm to **2 mm**, so the margin of error is smaller (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- Patients between sizes led to gender-specific implants
- Femoral sizing in theatre → 08 Technique

### Principle of Constraint
Constraint is how much the implant, rather than the ligaments, holds the knee together.

#### The Trade-off
- More constraint gives more stability but less motion
- The load then moves from the soft tissues to the fixation
- So the rule is the **least constraint** that gives a balanced knee
- Constraint replaces **absent** ligaments, never tight ones; tight ones are released

MEMORY HOOK — the seat belt bolted to bone
- Constraint is a seat belt bolted to the bone: the tighter the belt, the harder it pulls the bolts (the fixation).

#### The Constraint Ladder
| Class | Design | Stability comes from | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unconstrained | resurfacing, UKA | native ligaments | all ligaments intact |
| Unconstrained | CR | retained PCL | healthy, balanced PCL |
| (CR variant) | ultra-congruent (deep-dish) insert | dished insert, no post | PCL lost in a CR knee |
| Semi-constrained | PS | cam and post (AP only) | PCL absent or deficient |
| Constrained, non-linked | CCK | tall post in a deep box (+ varus–valgus) | weak but present collaterals |
| Constrained, linked | rotating hinge | hinge axle | global ligament loss |

- The Handbook names three classes: unconstrained, semi-constrained (PS only) and constrained
- CR counts as unconstrained, because its stability comes from the native PCL

#### Choosing the Level
- The **ultra-congruent** (deep-dish) insert gives AP stability without a post
- Choose the level with **trial inserts**
- Step up only if the knee is still unstable after balancing
- Standing films show coronal laxity, so they predict the level needed (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- With no constrained implant in theatre, the knee is left unstable or the operation incomplete

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when can a knee be unconstrained?"
- "**Unconstrained** designs rely on native ligaments, so the ligaments must be intact."
- "**UKA** replaces one condyle and its plateau, and it needs an intact **ACL**."
- "UKA fails more often than TKA in registries, but recovery is faster."

### Resurfacing
Resurfacing is the principle behind most modern knees.
- **Resurfacing** replaces the joint surfaces but keeps the ligaments
- No whole compartment is resected
- Condylar knees are resurfacing designs
[[FIG: Fig 7.7 · 7.3
- A UKA, like kinematic alignment, leaves a varus knee in varus
- Only the surface changes; the soft tissues are untouched

### Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty
A UKA (unicompartmental knee arthroplasty) is resurfacing confined to one compartment.

#### Candidates
- **UKA** replaces one condyle and its plateau
- Most UKAs are medial, because the medial compartment fails most
- The other compartments must be healthy, so RA (a general arthritis) is excluded
- It suits the elderly thin patient
- It also suits a younger patient as a "first" arthroplasty, instead of an **HTO** (high tibial osteotomy)

#### Selection Criteria
- **Kozinn and Scott** (1989) set strict criteria
- Disease in one compartment, with a correctable deformity and an intact **ACL**
- A small contracture and good motion

#### Contraindications
- Inflammatory arthritis, **ACL** deficiency or opposite-compartment erosion
- Flexion contracture **≥15°**, or an arc of motion <90° (Campbell)
- Varus **>10°** or valgus >5° from the mechanical axis
- Obesity is only a relative contraindication
- Only **6%** of arthroplasty patients have no contraindication (Campbell)

PITFALL — UKA deformity limit
- The Handbook says "deformity >5–10°" with no plane; Campbell gives **>10° varus, >5° valgus**
- Say → "**UKA is out if varus >10°, valgus >5°, contracture ≥15° or arc <90°**"

MEMORY HOOK — the UKA phone number
- Dial **10-5-15-90** before a UKA: varus 10°, valgus 5°, contracture 15°, arc 90°. Any number over the line, hang up.

#### Survival
- The **Oxford** mobile-bearing UKA survives **94%** at 10 years (Campbell)
- It survives 91% at 20 years
- A robotic fixed-bearing medial UKA survives **91.7%** at 10 years (Campbell)
- Its revisions were for unexplained pain and loosening

#### Failure and Revision
- UKAs fail by **aseptic loosening**, arthritis progression or proximal tibial fracture
- Registries show **more revisions** than TKA, but a faster recovery and a more natural feel
- It is meant to be cheaper, but it may cost more and be harder to implant
- Revision to TKA needs special parts, grafts or augments in **45–76%** (Campbell)

7.4.b:
Most primary knees sit on the next two rungs, and the PCL decides which one.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "CR or PS: how do you choose?"
- "**CR** (cruciate-retaining) keeps the PCL, so it needs a healthy, **balanced** PCL."
- "**PS** (posterior-stabilised) sacrifices it: the **cam strikes the post** and forces rollback."
- "RA, PCL loss, patellectomy or a big deformity → **PS**."

### Cruciate-Retaining Design
A CR knee keeps the PCL and lets it do its native work.

#### Mechanism
- The retained **PCL** gives AP stability, femoral **rollback** and quadriceps efficiency
[[FIG: Fig 7.8 · 7.4
- Normal flexion is **rolling plus gliding**, so the contact point moves back (Prof Abd Elkarim)
[[FIG: Fig 7.9 · 7.4
- The PCL controls this rollback, holding the femur back on the tibia
[[FIG: Fig 7.10 · 7.4
- Rollback adds flexion, which stretches the quadriceps, so they work better
- The CR insert is flatter, so it allows rollback
- A conforming insert with a retained PCL would impinge posteriorly

#### Failure Modes
- Without a working PCL in deep flexion, the femur rolls off the back and impinges
- A tight PCL stresses the knee at each flexion, so the tray **lifts off** (seesaw) and loosens
- Tight or loose PCL, recession and conversion to PS → 09 Balancing

#### Keeping the PCL
- For: a native PCL replicates the anatomy (Prof Shokry)
- Against: a degenerate PCL may rupture later
- In Egypt patients present late, so PCL health is doubtful
- A late rupture then fails the whole knee

### Posterior-Stabilised Design
A PS knee sacrifices the PCL and replaces it with a cam and a post.

#### Mechanism
- With the PCL gone, the femoral **cam engages the tibial post** and forces rollback
[[FIG: Fig 7.11 · 7.4
- The cam does not brake on the post; it pivots on it for an extra push
- The post resists posterior translation only
- Coronal stability still comes from the collaterals, so a PS knee cannot answer an absent MCL
- The box cut removes extra femoral bone, which matters at revision
- A CR knee needs no box, so it keeps that bone: the "CR privilege"

#### Indications
- The PCL is absent or deficient
- The patient has RA: pannus weakens the ligaments and capsule
- The PCL was released for a big deformity, or the patient had a **patellectomy**
- Most surgeons choose **PS**, because CR balancing is much harder early in a career (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- Prof Shokry sacrifices the PCL in all: his patients come late, with poor soft tissues

MEMORY HOOK — the doorstop
- The PS post is a doorstop: in flexion the cam hits it, and the femur is pushed back (rollback).

### Comparison of CR and PS Designs
The Handbook sets the two side by side, and examiners ask the table.

#### Key Differences
| Feature | PS | CR |
|---|---|---|
| **Cam–post** | cam strikes post → rollback | none |
| **Insert** | conforming (dished) | flatter → allows rollback |
| **Indication** | RA, PCL injury | intact PCL, no RA |
| **X-ray** | box, larger femoral cut | normal pegs |
| **Proprioception** | inferior | superior (native PCL) |
| **Flexion** | ≈120° | 105–110° |
| **Wear** | lower, load spread | higher, point contact |
| **Late failure** | post wear, cam jump | late PCL rupture → instability |

#### Evidence
- Studies show a difference of ≈**4°** in favour of CR, maybe not significant (Prof Abd Elkarim)
- So the PCL policy is the surgeon's philosophy, and both are correct
- Fluoroscopy shows **paradoxical anterior sliding** in many CR knees, so CR rollback is less reliable
- A retained PCL is tensioned unlike a native one after TKA
- So PS rollback is closer to normal, and the Handbook gives PS more flexion
- But long-term flexion of CR and PS is similar in most studies (Campbell)

#### Insert Geometry
- Early flat CR inserts had high contact stress, so they wore
[[FIG: Fig 7.12 · 7.4
- Newer CR inserts are more conforming
- Slope by design → 08 Technique

### Design-Specific Complications
Each design fails in its own way: PS at the post, CR at the PCL and the insert.

#### Cam Jump and Post Wear
- **Cam jump** follows a loose flexion gap
- In deep flexion, ± varus–valgus stress, the cam slips over the post
- Prevent it by balancing the flexion gap; treat it by revision
- **Post wear** or breakage comes when the femoral component hits the post in hyperextension
[[FIG: Fig 7.13 · 7.4
- Impingement rises with a flexed femoral component, more slope and hyperextension
- Cement left in the notch touches the post, so the knee loosens early

#### Patellar Clunk
- A nodule at the quadriceps tendon–superior pole junction catches in the box: **patellar clunk**
- It clunks at **30–45°** of flexion on active extension (Campbell)
- The scar is excised arthroscopically or open
- Causes: proximal button overhang, or a box that starts below the trochlea
- A longer trochlea makes it rarer

#### CR Wear and Late PCL Failure
- The less conforming CR insert has higher contact stress, so it wears faster
- A tight PCL makes the condyles ride the posterior polyethylene lip: extreme stress
- A posterior sag or drawer years after a CR knee means **late PCL insufficiency**

#### Long-term Survival
- At the **Mayo Clinic**, 15-year survival of PS knees was **77%** (2728 knees) (Campbell)
- CR knees survived **90%** (5389 knees)

PITFALL — which design wears more and fails late?
- The Handbook files wear and PCL failure under PS complications, but both belong to **CR**
- Say → "**CR: the flat insert wears more and the PCL may rupture late · PS: post wear, cam jump, clunk**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **CR = balanced PCL, slope in bone · PS = cam–post, slope in insert, box · clunk at 30–45°**

7.5.b:
When the collaterals or the bone fail, constraint moves up the ladder: first a taller post, then a hinge.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "when do you need more constraint?"
- "**CCK** is a PS with a tall, wide post in a deep box: it needs weak but present collaterals."
- "A **rotating hinge** is linked, with free rotation: for global ligament loss, tumour or salvage."
- "More constraint means more load on fixation, so constrained knees get **stems**."

### Indications for Constraint
Constrained designs add varus–valgus control to AP stability.
- They are for deficient collaterals or massive bone loss
- Most are used in **revision**, a valgus knee with an incompetent MCL, or a neuropathic or post-traumatic knee
- More constraint loads the fixation more, so **stems** share the load
- Some systems stem the femur only in revision sets; primary sets stem the tibia only (Prof Sherif Khaled)

#### Stems in a Primary Knee
- Stem a primary tibia for varus **>15°**, obesity or osteoporosis
- Obesity and osteoporosis as reasons are still debated
- So template the stem; an unplanned, unavailable stem means a non-ideal component
[[FIG: Fig 7.14 · 7.5

### Constrained Condylar Knee
The CCK (constrained condylar knee) is the first step above PS, and it still has no link.

#### Design
- A **CCK** is a modified PS, with a larger post and a deeper box
[[FIG: Fig 7.15 · 7.5
- The post against the box walls controls varus–valgus, with a small toggle
- Otherwise it acts as a PS
- On film it looks like a PS with a deeper box, a taller, wider post, and usually **stems**

#### Indications
- The post and fixation take the ligament loads, so the collaterals must be **weak but present**
- Use it in revision with instability, or in a primary with extreme valgus and **MCL** insufficiency
- Stems are cemented or modular press-fit
- A mobile-bearing option lowers the tibial forces

#### Limits and Outcomes
- A CCK cannot block **recurvatum**
- More constraint means less motion and more aseptic loosening
- So loosening is feared in the young
- Primary CCKs had a revision rate of **0.8%** (Campbell)
- Their 10-year survival was **97.6%**

### Rotating-Hinge Knee
When the collaterals are absent, only a link between femur and tibia will hold.

#### Design
- A **hinge** links the femur to the tibia, so it blocks recurvatum
- Fixed hinges failed, because without rotation the torque went into the bone
- A rotating bearing dissipates that torque
- It is locked sagittally and coronally, but free in axial rotation, so interface force falls

#### Hinge Mechanisms
| Design | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Endo-model** | femoral bush between the condyles + tibial stem |
| **Kinematic / Noiles** | femoral axle, fixed by a transverse pin, rotates in a tibial sleeve |
| **S-ROM** | axle rotates in a stemmed polyethylene insert |
| **NexGen rotating hinge** | axle hangs free between the condyles → tibial stem: flexion, extension, rotation |
| **Kinematic Rotating Hinge** | 2 polyethylene + CoCr bearings: flexion–extension + axial rotation |

#### Indications
- **Global ligament deficiency**, or bone loss at the collateral origins
- Distal femoral tumour resection
- An elderly distal femoral nonunion or periprosthetic fracture
- Hyperextension instability, or a flexion–extension gap mismatch
- **Neuromuscular disease** and limb salvage; a **Charcot** knee gets a rotating hinge and a brace
- In a primary, only if the flexion gap may "jump" a CCK, because outcomes are worse

MEMORY HOOK — the bodyguard and the handcuffs
- A CCK is a bodyguard: it helps weak collaterals but needs them present. A hinge is handcuffs: it holds alone.

#### Outcomes
- The early Kinematic hinge was no better than **GUEPAR**
- The **S-ROM** had far fewer complications
- Complications: **infection**, loosening, extensor mechanism problems and hinge failure

PITFALL — CCK or hinge?
- A CCK needs **some** collateral function and a stable flexion gap, and it cannot stop recurvatum
- Say → "**Weak collaterals → CCK · absent collaterals, recurvatum or gap mismatch → rotating hinge**"

7.6.b:
Constraint is one way to sort knees; compartment coverage and bearing mobility are the other two.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how else are knee prostheses classified?"
- "By coverage: uni, **bicompartmental** (medial + PF), **bicondylar** (medial + lateral), tricompartmental."
- "By bearing: a **fixed** insert locked to the tray, or a **mobile** insert rotating on it."
- "A mobile insert can **spin out** if the gaps are unbalanced."

### Compartment Coverage
The implant should cover the compartments that are diseased, and no fewer.

#### Coverage Classes
| Class | Replaced |
|---|---|
| **Unicompartmental** | one compartment |
| **Bicompartmental** | medial + patellofemoral |
| **Bicondylar** | medial + lateral |
| **Tricompartmental** (= conventional TKA) | medial + lateral + patellofemoral |

- So check every compartment before choosing, the **patellofemoral** included

#### Patellofemoral Arthroplasty
- A **PFA** (patellofemoral arthroplasty) treats isolated PF arthritis, often with trochlear dysplasia
- The ideal patient is <65 years old, with minimal coronal deformity
- Avoid it in valgus >8°, varus >5° (unless osteotomy), or inflammatory arthritis
- The main cause of conversion is **tibiofemoral** progression
- In the elderly with severe PF arthritis, **TKA** beats patellectomy or PFA

### Bearing Mobility
The insert can be locked to the tray or left free to rotate on it.

#### Fixed and Mobile Bearings
- A **fixed** bearing locks the insert to the tray
- A **mobile** bearing lets the insert rotate on a polished tray
[[FIG: Fig 7.16 · 7.6
- It turns part of the femoral load into motion on the tray
- In theory it lowers contact stress, allows rotation in gait and self-aligns small tray malrotation
- It was once chosen for the young, for less wear
- But a balanced fixed bearing lasts as long (Prof Shokry)
- He no longer uses mobile bearings

#### Technical Pitfalls
- The insert follows the **femur**, so tray, insert and femur are set together on a diathermy mark
- If the tibia is rotated unlike the femur, the insert sits **15°** off, prominent, and arthrofibrosis follows
- A fixed tray takes rotation from curve-on-curve, the tuberosity line or the rod
- A mobile tray takes it from the diathermy mark instead
- A postoperative **click** is mostly the patella on the anterior femoral flange
- It is commoner with mobile bearings: a very free insert or poorly set rotation
- The **LCS** (low contact stress) knee uses the tibial cut as its rotation reference, so it needs good balance

MEMORY HOOK — the dog on a lead
- A mobile insert follows the femur like a dog follows its owner, so set tray, insert and femur on one mark.

#### Complications and Evidence
- **Spin-out** (rotational dislocation) follows unbalanced gaps; **backside wear** is the other problem
- A spun-out insert needs open reduction and a thicker insert
- If the gaps are unbalanced, revise instead
- The lower-wear claim is now doubtful
- The evidence shows more short- and midterm revisions, but one meta-analysis found no difference

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **CCK = tall post + stems · hinge rotates, blocks recurvatum · bicompartmental = medial + PF · mobile → spin-out**
